26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.51:
A performance round, on the GPU side of the terrain pixel. Your Adreno 640 draws a 12-chunk view at 1080p, and the terrain fragment stage was the most expensive thing in it: every minified terrain pixel paid nine texture fetches (one plain plus the game's own four-tap rotated grid at two mip levels each) to fight shimmer that, that far out, the arithmetic already answers for free.

- **The far field stops paying the grid's bill**: the rotated grid's taps sit 0.395 of a fine texel off centre, and at eight texels a pixel that is under five per cent of one coarse texel - so past that line two fetches (one bilinear at each level, blended by the same fraction) return what the eight returned, to within what a screen cannot resolve. Most of a loaded view is past that line: expect the far three-quarters of the terrain pixels to draw at two fetches instead of nine.
- **The near field keeps the grid**: below the line the texel edge is screen-sized and the grid is the anti-aliasing - nothing changes where shimmer is actually visible. Magnified surfaces also skip the level math they never read, and the minified middle band stops fetching the plain texel it was multiplying by zero.
- **The two terrain shaders carry the tiers together**, and a test now holds them to it: their sampling code has to stay identical file for file, or the solid and cutout layers would seam at the tier line.
- **A log lie fixed on the way**: the arena's "it cannot grow" verdict compared the pool's total size against one buffer's cap, so on your device it said cannot-grow with thirty more buffers of headroom left. Informational only - the rebuild was never gated on it - but every trim line you sent was carrying it.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.50:
Your android.49 log caught the bug that has been eating worlds whole - the one reported as "some places are transparent / not rendered". The renderer obeyed the game's occlusion list even when that list was empty or named nothing the arena holds, and your log shows thirty-five straight seconds of a 526-section world drawing nothing at all before quit.

- **The blank world, explained**: the game's visibility snapshot is only refilled when the camera turns two degrees or its occlusion graph moves. When one refill came back empty - and the camera then held still - the snapshot never refilled, and the terrain pass culled every section it held with an answer about none of them. The arena had the world; the pass refused to draw it. Both renderers went blank together, which is why nothing else in the log looked wrong.
- **The fix**: a list that is empty, or that names no section the arena can actually draw, is now read as "no list" for that frame - the frustum decides instead, exactly as it does before the first list of a session arrives. Over-draw replaces the hole, and the occlusion culling itself is untouched on every frame the list genuinely answers about the arena (the trust check exits on the first named section, so healthy frames pay nothing for it).
- **Visible in the log**: the once-a-second frustum line now ends with "N frame(s) that drew from the frustum because the game's list was empty or named nothing the arena holds" - a wedged graph is now a climbing number instead of an invisible world. If you see the world go blank again, that number and the log are the report.
- **Fabric side audited**: the per-tick hooks (block cache, camera pin, debug reload) all early-return on cached settings and empty queues, and both loaders share one render path - there is no Fabric-specific frame cost to remove. The batching android.49 delivered stands.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.49:
android.48's safety probe turned out to be the very thing standing between your phone and the fast path. This build takes the gate off its back and hardens the probe under it.

- **What your log showed**: the floor probe read clear colour back (`[200, 200, 200, 200]`) and closed the batched terrain before the real probes ever ran - while the same driver rasterised ~15,000 terrain draws a frame for the game itself. The batched path was proven-safe by a probe that could not prove anything, and your device drew one section at a time at full draw-call cost.
- **The gate is gone**: the channel probes (first-instance for the game path, index-record for the terrain's exact batched shape) now **always run**, and each one that reads its own sentinels back has proven the methodology for itself - no floor beneath them required. The floor stays as a diagnostic, and a failed channel still closes its own path: the probe system's protection is intact, only the false negative is gone.
- **The probe methodology itself was rebuilt**, because an all-clear readback on a device whose game rasterises fine is the probe lying, not the driver: the render pass and the readback copy are now **separate submissions** (a tiler can no longer race the copy past the draws), the target is 64 pixels wide instead of the 4 pixels the quads minimally cover, the probe's data is written through both upload paths, and on a failure the vertex buffer itself is read back so the log says whether the draws never rasterised or their data never landed.
- **If the index-record probe passes** (the log says 'the index-record probe drew four records through one multi-draw'), the terrain batches: one multi-draw per run of sections instead of hundreds of draw calls - the big one on Adreno.
- **If it still fails**, the log now carries three readbacks (target, vertex buffer, probe channel) that pin the exact stage - send the log and the next build fixes the named stage.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.48:
The batched terrain path was closed by its own safety probe - and the probe was asking the wrong question. This build re-asks it on the target your game actually draws onto.

- **What the log showed**: every release since the probes went in read the same answer on Adreno 640 - `[999, 999, 999, 999]`, the clear colour, off every pixel of every probe. The verdict was 'this driver cannot batch', and the terrain fell back to hundreds of draw calls a frame.
- **What was wrong with that**: the probes rendered onto `R32Uint`, an integer target the game itself never asks for - the whole game is drawn onto the swapchain's `Rgba8Unorm`. The same batched call had demonstrably rasterised on this very device back when the game drew with it, so the one thing the probes and the batched path did not share - the target format - was the likeliest place for the verdict to come from. A mobile tile-based driver quietly not rasterising onto an integer target is a known class of fault, and it looks exactly like 'the batched call is broken' when the probe is the only thing using that target.
- **The change**: the probes now ask on `Rgba8Unorm`. A **floor probe** (four plain `draw_indexed` calls of a trivial pipeline) proves the methodology first, and its verdict gates the channel probes; the `R32Uint` question runs as a forensic beside it, so the next log names which one was lying. If the floor draws and the batched shape draws on Rgba8Unorm, the terrain batches - a handful of draw calls a frame instead of hundreds to thousands.
- **Also**: the per-second claim report now carries the bake-waiter count, so a gap between 'sections claimed' and 'sections drawn' can be read as bakes backing up rather than guessed at.

If terrain still draws one section at a time, the log now says exactly which probe failed and what it read back - send the log.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.47:
Fabric still left the world at the login packet - one layer deeper than android.46's fix. The class now transforms, and the crash moved to the next claimant of the same instruction.

- **What the log showed**: `@Redirect conflict. Skipping fabric-renderer-api-v1...` right before `InjectionError: Critical injection failure: Redirector tesselateBlockProxy ... (0/1) succeeded. Scanned 0 target(s)` inside `Mixin transformation of net.minecraft.client.renderer.chunk.SectionCompiler failed` - disconnect, then the crash screen. NeoForge was never affected: Indigo is a Fabric-side renderer.
- **The cause**: fabric-renderer-api-v1 (Indigo, in fabric-api on every Fabric install) redirects the same `tesselateBlock` call inside the same `SectionCompiler.compile` this mod redirected - that call site is the seam its own renderer hangs on, by design. Two `@Redirect`s cannot share an instruction: Mixin handed the instruction to one of them (ours won), and the loser's `require` check then threw, which is a class that refuses to transform. The android.46 signature fix is what let the class get as far as this collision - the two bugs stacked in front of each other.
- **The fix**: the `tesselateBlock` redirect is gone, and it was redundant, not load-bearing: the `getRenderShape` predicate redirect already decides the same answer in the same block iteration (both read the same per-thread bake answer), so while Rust owns the section the whole `== MODEL` body - the call site included - never executes, and when Rust does not own it, Indigo's proxy runs exactly as it would without this mod. No branch of anything changed; the claim that bought the crash did.
- **The gate this ships behind**: a second CI audit now reads fabric-api's *compiled* mixin classes from the pinned release players run (0.155.3+26.1.2), cross-checks every instruction both mods claim, and fails the build on any overlap that is not two plain `@Inject`s - the android.46 audit resolved our targets against the game's jar; this one resolves them against the other mods', which is the half it could not see.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.46:
Fabric could load the mod, reach a world, and then be thrown out of it: the chunk-compile mixin pinned NeoForge's five-argument compile signature, which vanilla does not have, and a mixin whose target cannot be found is a class that refuses to transform.

- **What the log showed**: `Mixin apply for mod wgpu_mc failed ... SectionCompilerMixin` followed by `Mixin transformation of net.minecraft.client.renderer.chunk.SectionCompiler failed` the moment a world joined - `LevelRenderer.allChanged` loads that class, the load threw, the login packet was dropped, and the client disconnected and hit the crash screen. NeoForge was never affected: its patch is what adds the fifth `List` argument the mixin was pinned to.
- **The fix**: every injection in that mixin now names both signatures - the four-argument one vanilla (and Fabric) runs, and the five-argument one NeoForge patched in - and Mixin applies whichever the running loader actually has. The two callbacks that used to capture the compile's arguments now capture none of them (Mixin takes all of a target's arguments or none, so an argument-capturing handler pinned to either loader could not serve both); the region and section they need come from a per-thread rebuild context the task hook sets before the compile runs. Nothing else about the path changed: the geometry skip, the occlusion mask and the block-entity hand-over behave as before on both loaders.
- **What that changes on Fabric**: until now every Fabric section rebuild built Minecraft's own geometry in full and threw it away, on top of the Rust bake - the mixin that skips that build could not apply. With it applying, a Fabric rebuild does what a NeoForge rebuild does: one bake, no second mesher, and the per-block work of a compile is the mask pass.
- **The gate this ships behind**: a CI step now resolves every `method =`, `target =`, `@Accessor` and `@Invoker` string in both mixins.json files against the real vanilla client jar before any build runs, so a mixin pinned to one loader's patched signature cannot ship silently again.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.45:
The batching the driver was refused: wgpu's indirect-draw validation was zeroing its own rewritten arguments on the Adreno drivers, and the probes read their clear colour and turned the batched terrain path off for a fault the driver does not have.

- **What the logs showed**: both probes read `[999, 999, 999, 999]` - the clear colour, not the records they drew - so the terrain pass fell back to drawing sections one contiguous run at a time: ~18,000 sections a frame in a few hundred runs, and the moment the run count drifted over the 256 rail, thousands of blits instead. Every counter agreed the world was being drawn; the frame cost was what disagreed.
- **The fix**: wgpu's indirect validation - the compute pass it injects ahead of every indirect draw to bounds-check the arguments - is off by default on Android now. The draws read the arguments this renderer wrote and bounded itself, and the defaults migration moves the carried `on` aside the way vsync and the batching switch moved before; turning it back on holds as a diagnosis choice. Desktops keep the check.
- **What that re-opens**: if the probes now read their four sentinels back in order, the batched path draws a whole terrain pass in one multi-draw command - a few commands a frame where the fallback paid hundreds of draws or thousands of copies. The boot log will say so: `the index-record probe ... read its sentinels back in order`.
- **Also**: the in-place run rail moved 256 to 1024, so a loaded world (which plans 258-324 runs) stops straddling it and paying the compacted draw's blit traffic on alternate frames.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.44:
The self-contained jar: the NeoForge `-all` build now carries Kotlin for Forge, and the Fabric build loads at all.

- **NeoForge: no separate KFF install any more.** The `-all` jar embedded the Kotlin stdlib but still demanded Kotlin for Forge as a separate download - a name that promised dependencies and shipped half of them. The four KFF artifacts (the Kotlin runtime carrier, the `kotlinforforge` mod itself, its library and the language provider `modLoader=` resolves to) now ride inside the jar under `META-INF/jarjar/`, so a fresh install needs exactly one file. **One migration step if an older Kotlin for Forge is still in `mods/`: remove it once after updating.** The loader refuses two mods with the same id, and both the old KFF and this jar declare `kotlinforforge`.
- **Fabric: the mod loads.** The Fabric entrypoint was a Kotlin `object`, whose constructor compiles private - and Fabric's language adapter instantiates entrypoints with a plain reflective `newInstance()` that cannot touch a private constructor, so every launch died with `IllegalAccessException ... modifiers "private"` before one line of the mod ran. The entrypoint is a class now, and the loader constructs it like any other. Fabric keeps its one external dependency: fabric-api, as usual.
- **Fabric builds hold the release now.** The Fabric job graduated from `continue-on-error`: a Fabric compile break stops the release instead of shipping a NeoForge-only jar under a version the update checker calls current, and both jars' content checks are strict.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.41:
The shredded-world fix: android.40's alignment change made the compacted terrain draw tear the geometry apart, and this build stops the tear at its source.

- **What you saw: a world of stretched, shredded triangles.** android.40 rounded every arena allocation to a multiple of four words so the terrain shaders could load vertices as whole vectors - the change that fixed the per-vertex load storm. But six indices a quad only lands on a four-word boundary for every second section, so the odd sections carried two spare words at the end of their index range, holding whatever the previous section had left there. One section drawing alone never completed a triangle out of them. The compacted draw - the path this renderer's phones actually draw with - packs sections back to back into one index buffer, and those two words sat *between* two sections' real indices: from the first slack word on, every triangle of the run was three wrong vertices, and the two spare words themselves were stale index values pointing into recycled sections. A world of long black spikes is what that reads as.
- **The fix: draws measure indices exactly as baked.** The allocation stays rounded - that is the vec4 contract, and the shaders lean on it - but the exact baked count now travels beside it, and every consumer measures draws with it: the compacted draw's copies and destinations, the one-draw-per-section fallback, the batched indirect records. A section's indices now end in the buffer exactly where the next section's begin, and every triangle the GPU reads is a quad the bake wrote.
- **Pinned by tests so it cannot come back quietly**: the arena records both counts and the gap between them, and the copy planner asserts every section's destination lands on a triangle boundary.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.40:
The deep rendering pass: the terrain vertex stage does a quarter of the memory work it did, and every vertex carries less to every fragment.

- **The terrain vertex stage loads 4 words a vertex where it loaded 9.** The stage fetched all of its geometry out of the section arena with storage-buffer loads - four scalars for the vertex itself, four more for the quad's four ambient-occlusion corners, and the section record - and the corner loads were the same four words for every vertex of a quad. The arena's vertex data is now loaded one whole vector per vertex, and the bake packs the four corner counts into one word per quad that all four vertices share; the section record moved to two whole vectors for the same reason. This is the one stage that runs per vertex, and load/store pressure there is what tile-based mobile GPUs (Mali in particular) are shortest of - this is the change aimed at the 'performance does not match the hardware' gap, not a tweak.
- **Every fragment reads five varyings where it read eleven.** The four ambient-occlusion corners are one packed u32 now (the fragment unpacks them with three shifts), and the four face flags - which atlas, animated, mipped cutout, level-of-detail floor - are one more. The picture is unchanged: same numbers, same blend, one quarter of the interpolation traffic.
- **The arena keeps the vec4 contract.** Every range the arena hands out is now a multiple of four words, so the shaders' vector addressing is exact by construction; a section costs one slot per quad more than before (the packed corner word), and the render-distance sizing constant accounts for it.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.39:
The iOS crash from the last report, fixed; two renderer savings on Android.

- **iOS: "can only access UIView on the main thread" - the renderer could not be created.** The android.38 fix got the mod loading on iOS (the dylib is found, the launcher's game view reaches the Rust side), but the first device creation then panicked inside the Metal window glue: wgpu asks the game view for its render layer through code that refuses to touch a UIView off the main thread, and Prisma runs the game on a background thread. The one call that touches the view is dispatched onto the process main queue now and waited for - once per renderer, at a moment the main thread is idle in the launcher's run loop - and everything after it works on the CAMetalLayer, which is documented thread-safe. First real-device run past device creation: report what the log says.
- **Android: the compacted terrain draw no longer re-copies its index data every frame.** The compacted draw blits the frame's index ranges out of the arena every frame before drawing them as one call per run - several megabytes of blits a frame even when nothing changed. Each terrain pass now owns its own compacted buffer, and a frame whose copy plan is byte-for-byte what the pass blitted last - over an arena whose mutation counter has not moved - skips the blits and draws the buffer as it stands. Standing still or turning in place in a settled world, the copies drop to zero; a bake, a trim, or a pool change moves the counter and the copies come back for that frame. The counter lives on the arena storage behind the lock the mutations already hold, so a cached plan cannot outlive the ranges it names.
- **Android: the refuse-and-resend accounting warns no more.** Cutting the render distance handed sections back through the same channel a refusal uses, but never counted them as refused - the JVM checked its sum and read `-324 unaccounted for`. A trim drop is counted where the hand-over is fed from now, and regression tests hold the sequence.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.38:
Two crashes from the field reports, both found and fixed from your logs.

- **Android: the game aborted seconds into a world ("index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0", then "failed to initiate panic, error 5").** The arena keeps two free-list rings that must stay the same length - one for the geometry ranges, one for the record slots - and they are cleared together by the render-distance report every world's first frame runs. The first fresh bake of a world has no old section to replace, so the records side had nothing to queue and skipped its ring entirely - while the ranges side minted its ring's first bucket anyway. The next frame's rotation then walked the records ring one bucket past its end, and a panic through the JNI frame is the process gone. The rings are minted in pairs now, and a regression test replays the exact sequence (report, fresh bake, rotation) so it cannot come back quietly.
- **iOS: the game crashed at startup ("A required function is missing: glfwGetX11Display").** The launcher's GLFW shim answers X11 whatever actually runs underneath - Minecraft's own GLX init asks for X11 by name - so the mod trusted it, walked into LWJGL's X11 function table, and died in class init because the launcher's GLFW has no X11 functions. The pointer the renderer wants was never a GLFW accessor anyway: Prisma/Amethyst publish the game's UIView pointer at launch as the `metallum.ios.view.pointer` property (the same one the Metallum Metal path reads), and the mod now takes that and hands it straight to the Rust side's UiKit surface branch. A launcher without the property gets a backend error screen naming the property instead of a crash. First real-device Metal run - report what the log says.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.35:
Three things landed in this build: the terrain's batched draw finally reaches the phones whose drivers refused it, the jar is multi-platform again (iOS included), and the frame now has named insertion points for Iris-style passes.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.34:
The corruption that survived the last two fixes has its root cause, and it is one line long: the section-record table's batched uploads handed every run after the first the FIRST run's bytes. Fixed, with a contract test that pins it.

- **What you saw.** Stretched black shards and misplaced white slabs that moved around between frames - the picture the 32-chunk screenshots are full of, still present on android.33.
- **Why.** The terrain shader reads each section's record (its origin and where its vertices live) out of a table, addressed by the section's own index words. The table is uploaded per frame in runs of adjacent slots to keep the write count down. The gathering recorded where the FIRST run's bytes sit and pushed a hardcoded zero for every later run - so run two, three, four wrote the first run's records at their own slots. Every section in those runs then fetched somebody else's vertices at somebody else's position: geometry nobody baked, drawn wherever the foreign record pointed. Which sections corrupted moved with each frame's run layout, which is why it flickered and never matched a single cause.
- **The fix.** Each run now records its own byte position when it opens - the arena's own uploads always did, which is what makes this divergence visible in hindsight. A contract test draws three scattered runs and asserts every run's window is its own records.
- **Iris/Vulkan research updated (docs/iris-adaptation-research.md section 4.6).** The Iris 1.12.0-snapshot jar circulating in the wild is the official Vulkan rewrite in development: a backend abstraction with OpenGL and Vulkan implementations, riding Minecraft 26.x's own native Vulkan renderer, compiling pack GLSL to SPIR-V with shaderc. The released Iris (1.11.7) has none of this. Separately, Vitrail already loads OptiFine-format packs on Minecraft's native Vulkan renderer, NeoForge included - the first shipping proof that 'Vulkan renderer + OptiFine packs' works. What it means for this mod is written down in the doc.

If any corruption remains, send the log - but this one was reproducible in the records themselves, and the test fails on the old code.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.33:
The stretched-terrain corruption - long thin triangles shooting into the sky while a world loads - is closed on the renderer's own paths, and both fixes count and log themselves so a field log can name any remaining culprit.

- **Where the streaks came from.** A baked index is `(record_slot << 17) | local_vertex`, and the shader reads the section's record out of the high bits. Two ways to draw wrong geometry: a bake whose local vertex id ran past the 17 bits the format holds (the guard for this was a `debug_assert`, which a release build compiles away - the spill silently shifted the record slot and fetched another section's vertices at this one's transform), and a rebuild the pool refused whose replaced record slots were freed anyway - the kept section then read whoever took the slot next. Both are exactly the picture the 32-chunk screenshot showed: triangles stretched across the world, chunks in the wrong place, black fragments.
- **The fixes.** Every bake's indices are now checked while they are still plain local ids - one pass over memory the packing loop walks anyway - and an overflow refuses the bake, keeps the section's game mesh, counts itself, and says so on the log with the position and the layer. The replaced records are no longer deferred on a refused replacement: the deferral belongs to the replacement, not to the attempt. Two contract tests pin both behaviours.
- **What 32 chunks really costs, measured.** The session's numbers: the 32-chunk view asks the arena for 1.09 GB, the record table's ceiling holds it at 512 MB, and until the pool fills the game meshes the rest - which at 97% device memory is the freeze. Until the distance-capped fallback lands, 16-20 chunks is the setting this device can hold.
- **Iris research updated with market evidence.** VulkanMod's own shader answer is Beryl - which ships an integrated shader pack and loads no Iris packs at all. The doc now records it: the Vulkan-native pipeline route has a working precedent, and pack compatibility remains the one unsolved hard problem (docs/iris-adaptation-research.md, section 4.5).

If streaks ever come back, send the log: a line starting `a bake at (x, y, z)` names the section, the layer and how far past the cliff the mesher reached.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.32:
The distant-terrain corruption - the flat black band over the ocean - is fixed: Minecraft's own mesh now stays until the Rust bake has actually landed.

- **What the black band was, in the log's own numbers.** Minecraft's mesh for a section was dropped the moment the Rust baker accepted its payload - but accepting is queueing, and the bake queue drains at about thirty sections a second. A 32-chunk world needs tens of thousands of them, so every section sat with no game mesh and no arena geometry for minutes: a band of terrain drawn by nobody. Over an ocean that is a flat void-coloured plane where the sea should be - the corruption reported at 12 chunks in flight and at 32 chunks standing still, on every build since batching shipped.
- **The gate moved from the offer to the publish.** A section keeps Minecraft's own mesh until its bake has landed in the arena - the world is drawn by the game's own path from the first seconds, and each section hands over to the Rust terrain exactly once, when the arena can actually draw it. The publish reaches the JVM through a new per-tick drain (`publishedSections`, the mirror of the refusal drain); the first publish of a section queues one rebuild that retires the game's mesh. Refused, trimmed and parked sections all keep or regain the game's mesh - a picture drawn by the slower renderer, never a picture missing.
- **No re-bake loop.** A rebuild that retires a mesh carries no changed blocks, and a published section whose payload has nothing to say no longer calls the baker at all - so the publish drain converges instead of cycling rebuild-and-rebake forever. The per-second terrain line now separates the two states: `N of the claims published` (the arena draws them) against the claims still waiting for their bake.
- **Loading looks different on purpose.** At extreme view distances the far field stays on Minecraft's own meshes until the arena reaches it - correct and slower, and the handover is progressive rather than a band of holes. The Iris adaptation research this session produced is checked in at docs/iris-adaptation-research.md.

The render-distance switch can no longer ask a phone for more memory than the draws can name.

- **What the 32-chunk report actually was, in the log's own numbers.** Switching the view to 32 chunks asked the section arena for 285,660,000 slots and was granted all of it - ten buffers, 1,216 MB - while holding 22M slots (6%, 83 MB). - **The fix: the arena stops at what the record table can name.** Every drawn section names itself through one 32,768-slot record table, and past that table's reach no amount of extra arena can be drawn - it is only memory. Distances phones run (8-20 chunks) pass through untouched; 22 and up come back as the ceiling, and the growth log says so in the same line ("... the view asked for 285,660,000 asked, 134,217,728 after the record table's ceiling").

With the arena no longer over-granted, the frame rate survives the load, the bake stream keeps up as it does at 12 chunks, and distant terrain fills in instead of staying hollow. A dense ocean world at extreme distances may still refuse sections into the vanilla path - that is the graceful answer, and it is one log line now ("N left to Minecraft because the arena is full").

World-black fix on Adreno 640, and the GLES option that works.

- The world was black from the first frame in it at a 12-chunk view. The section arena is bound as one storage buffer per arena, and a bind group binds a buffer entire: a 12-chunk view asked for a 192 MB pool, create_bind_group refuses any binding past max_storage_buffer_binding_size (128 MiB on the default limits), and what it leaves behind is an invalid bind group whose every use drops the whole frame - the terrain lines kept counting thousands of draws and none of them reached the GPU. The pool is split across buffers the binding can take now (128 MiB and the remainder), growth appends buffers under the same cap, and a buffer about to be bound oversized is a loud error instead of a black world.
- The renderer settings page's OpenGL ES option is attempted now instead of refused. ES 3.1 made vertex-stage storage buffers a required feature, which is what the arena reads; the attempt releases the launcher's hold on the shared window first, probes the context for vertex storage before anything is built, and falls back to Vulkan when the driver cannot. ES has no push constants, so the graph's terrain passes are not built there and the game draws its own meshes - slower than Vulkan, and the option for a device whose Vulkan driver wgpu cannot bring up.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.22:
GLES survives its first frame, and the buffers it binds are ones the driver will take.

- The GLES backend crashed at the first frame. The swapchain was configured with COPY_SRC - the usage that lets the presented image be read back for diagnostics - and a GL surface offers COLOR_TARGET only: the configure was refused, and the first acquire panicked with "Surface is not configured for presentation". The configure now asks for what the driver offers, and a driver without COPY_SRC turns the readback diagnostics off with a note instead of taking the swapchain down.
- Every ring uniform (transforms, chunk sections, lightmap, fog, cloud) and every GUI vertex buffer was refused on GLES. wgpu only lets MAP_WRITE share a usage mask with COPY_SRC unless the device advertises MAPPABLE_PRIMARY_BUFFERS - Vulkan adapters do, the GL backend never does - so on GLES the creation failed, every bind group on the buffer failed with it, and the frame drew without any of them. Nothing on this stack maps a buffer once it is created: every write travels through the staging path, so the JVM's masks are translated without the MAP bits that would sink the creation, and a mapped create is reserved for a pure staging mask. Four new tests pin the masks.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.28:
The performance release the last log pointed at: the section arena now grows to what the render distance actually asks for, and the threads this renderer owns run on the fast cores.

- **The arena grows again.** A render-distance report that arrived while the arena already held sections was supposed to grow it by appending another buffer, but the request was clamped to the size of a *single* buffer first - and on devices whose storage-binding limit makes one buffer smaller than the view (every Adreno at 12 chunks and up), the clamp left the request equal to what the arena already held, no growth was ever asked for, and sections the arena could not take were meshed by Minecraft's own path instead - the slower vertex format, drawn through the same GPU. The report is now clamped to the *pool's* ceiling (all buffers, under the memory budget), so a 12-chunk view gets the 192 MB it asks for across two buffers, and the sections that were falling back come back to the fast path.
- **Fragmentation now asks for room before it costs a section.** The growth trigger read how many slots were free; a churned arena holds its free slots as holes between held sections, so an arena at 39% held was refusing sections whose geometry had nowhere to sit - your log showed 909 of them. The trigger now also reads the longest *contiguous* free run, and appends a buffer while no run can take the largest section meshed so far. The refuse-then-re-mesh churn that shape produced is gone.
- **The render thread and the bake pool run on the performance cores.** On a big.LITTLE phone the scheduler parks whatever looks less busy on the slow cluster; the render thread now pins itself to the fast cores once, and the section-bake pool runs one thread per fast core, pinned there, leaving the efficiency cluster to the JVM's own background threads. Cluster detection is read from the device at runtime (cpufreq), and a device it cannot read keeps the old behaviour exactly.

If terrain ever goes missing after this build, that is a bug and not a culling choice - send the log. Nothing in this release changes what is drawn, only who meshes it and where it runs.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.29:
The batching release: the terrain draws in batches again on every device, including the one whose driver broke it.

- **What android.24-28 actually shipped, and what this fixes.** Every build since android.24 carried the batched terrain draw - one multi-draw indirect call per run of sections instead of one call per section - and every build since android.26 disabled it on Adreno 640, because the four-record probe this renderer runs at device creation proved that the driver accepts a non-zero `firstInstance` in an indirect record and then does not fetch the record it names. Your android.28 log says it plainly: "the first-instance probe did not read its sentinels back in order, and the terrain pass will not batch on this driver" - so the terrain kept drawing one section at a time, over a thousand calls a frame, and the 10% you measured came from the arena and core-pinning fixes alone. The batching itself never ran.
- **The record now travels in the indices.** A draw needs its section's position and its vertex range; all three previous channels for that - a storage binding indexed by `instance_index`, then an instance-step attribute offset by `first_instance` - died on the same driver. The one channel nothing can refuse is the index buffer itself: every baked index now carries the section's record slot in its high bits (`(slot << 17) | vertex`), and the vertex stage reads the record out of a per-bake table through those bits. The indirect record needs no per-draw data at all any more - `first_instance` and `base_vertex` are zero in every record, on every path, on every driver.
- **Per-frame record uploads are gone.** The records used to be rebuilt and re-uploaded for every visible section every frame (hundreds of kilobytes); they are written once per bake now, and the only per-frame upload left is the indirect argument list itself. The camera-relative offset the records used to carry is three integer subtractions in the shader.
- **The probe survives, and it guards the right thing.** The game's own repeated draws (entities, block entities) still batch through `first_instance`, so the probe now gates only that path: on a driver like this one the terrain batches and the game path draws one at a time - correct on both sides, and the terrain is the part that was slow.

Expected effect on the device the last log came from: the terrain pass goes from roughly a thousand draw calls a frame back to a handful of multi-draw calls, on top of the arena and core-pinning gains already measured. If geometry appears in the wrong place or the world draws hollow - the two signatures the old driver bug produced - send the log immediately; this build changes how every terrain vertex finds its section, and a wrong constant there is visible rather than subtle.

26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.42:
The terrain draws straight out of the arena, and the phone presents every frame it makes.

- **The gathering now prefers drawing in place.** The compacted draw - the shape every probe-refusing device runs - merges the frame's sections into contiguous runs, and then *copies* their index ranges into a per-frame buffer to draw them as one call. But a run that is already contiguous where it lives needs no copy at all: it is one plain `draw_indexed` over its own slice of the arena. That shape is the first choice now, the compacted draw (and its 16 MB buffers, which the logs watched grow 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8 -> 16 MB per slot) only takes over when a pass fragments past 256 runs, and a once-a-second line names any pass that crosses. Fifo, what vsync asks for, is a double-buffered queue: a frame that misses the display's refresh waits for the *next* one, so a GPU rendering at 45 fps presents at 30 - which reads as half the framerate the hardware should manage. The devices whose configs carry the old default get it flipped once; turning vsync back on holds from there. If a device still feels below its hardware after this update, check this switch first.

Both probes - first-instance and index-record - have been failing on Adreno 640 *and* Mali-G610, which is two vendors answering one question the same wrong way and no log line saying what any of them saw. 26.1.2.2612.0.8-android.52:
The renderer answers the FSR question the device has been asking: the frame is now rendered at a fraction of the window's resolution and stretched back over it, sharpened - the largest frame-time lever a phone has left.

- **Render scale (new setting, default 0.75 on Android, 1.0 elsewhere).** Everything the game draws - terrain, entities, water, sky, GUI - goes into one render target, and a tiler's fragment cost is per pixel: rendering at 0.75 hands back roughly forty percent of that work, which is the difference the far-field sampling change only began. 1.0 is the un-scaled picture, sampled one-to-one, exactly what previous builds made. Set it in the mod's own settings screen; it applies the moment Apply is pressed.
- **Upscale sharpening (new setting, default 0.5).** The present blit stretches the scaled frame back over the window with an unsharp mask over each sample's neighbourhood, so the picture keeps the crispness the window's own resolution would have had. Same jar as the 26.1.2 release of this build; the notes describe it once.

- **What you saw: a world of stretched, shredded triangles.** android.40 rounded every arena allocation to a multiple of four words so the terrain shaders could load vertices as whole vectors - the change that fixed the per-vertex load storm. But six indices a quad only lands on a four-word boundary for every second section, so the odd sections carried two spare words at the end of their index range, holding whatever the previous section had left there. One section drawing alone never completed a triangle out of them. The compacted draw - the path this renderer's phones actually draw with - packs sections back to back into one index buffer, and those two words sat *between* two sections' real indices: from the first slack word on, every triangle of the run was three wrong vertices, and the two spare words themselves were stale index values pointing into recycled sections. A world of long black spikes is what that reads as.
- **The fix: draws measure indices exactly as baked.** The allocation stays rounded - that is the vec4 contract, and the shaders lean on it - but the exact baked count now travels beside it, and every consumer measures draws with it: the compacted draw's copies and destinations, the one-draw-per-section fallback, the batched indirect records. A section's indices now end in the buffer exactly where the next section's begin, and every triangle the GPU reads is a quad the bake wrote.
- **Pinned by tests so it cannot come back quietly**: the arena records both counts and the gap between them, and the copy planner asserts every section's destination lands on a triangle boundary.

The arena's vertex data is now loaded one whole vector per vertex, and the bake packs the four corner counts into one word per quad that all four vertices share; the section record moved to two whole vectors for the same reason. This is the one stage that runs per vertex, and load/store pressure there is what tile-based mobile GPUs (Mali in particular) are shortest of - this is the change aimed at the 'performance does not match the hardware' gap, not a tweak.
- **Every fragment reads five varyings where it read eleven.** The four ambient-occlusion corners are one packed u32 now (the fragment unpacks them with three shifts), and the four face flags - which atlas, animated, mipped cutout, level-of-detail floor - are one more. The picture is unchanged: same numbers, same blend, one quarter of the interpolation traffic.

Standing still or turning in place in a settled world, the copies drop to zero; a bake, a trim, or a pool change moves the counter and the copies come back for that frame. The counter lives on the arena storage behind the lock the mutations already hold, so a cached plan cannot outlive the ranges it names.

The next frame's rotation then walked the records ring one bucket past its end, and a panic through the JNI frame is the process gone. The rings are minted in pairs now, and a regression test replays the exact sequence (report, fresh bake, rotation) so it cannot come back quietly.

The corruption that survived the last two fixes has its root cause, and it is one line long: the section-record table's batched uploads handed every run after the first the FIRST run's bytes. Fixed, with a contract test that pins it.

- **What you saw.** Stretched black shards and misplaced white slabs that moved around between frames - the picture the 32-chunk screenshots are full of, still present on android.33.

The table is uploaded per frame in runs of adjacent slots to keep the write count down. The gathering recorded where the FIRST run's bytes sit and pushed a hardcoded zero for every later run - so run two, three, four wrote the first run's records at their own slots. Every section in those runs then fetched somebody else's vertices at somebody else's position: geometry nobody baked, drawn wherever the foreign record pointed. Which sections corrupted moved with each frame's run layout, which is why it flickered and never matched a single cause.

The released Iris (1.11.7) has none of this. Separately, Vitrail already loads OptiFine-format packs on Minecraft's native Vulkan renderer, NeoForge included - the first shipping proof that 'Vulkan renderer + OptiFine packs' works. What it means for this mod is written down in the doc.

The stretched-terrain corruption - long thin triangles shooting into the sky while a world loads - is closed on the renderer's own paths, and both fixes count and log themselves so a field log can name any remaining culprit.

- **Where the streaks came from.** A baked index is `(record_slot << 17) | local_vertex`, and the shader reads the section's record out of the high bits. Two ways to draw wrong geometry: a bake whose local vertex id ran past the 17 bits the format holds (the guard for this was a `debug_assert`, which a release build compiles away - the spill silently shifted the record slot and fetched another section's vertices at this one's transform), and a rebuild the pool refused whose replaced record slots were freed anyway - the kept section then read whoever took the slot next. Both are exactly the picture the 32-chunk screenshot showed: triangles stretched across the world, chunks in the wrong place, black fragments.
- **The fixes.** Every bake's indices are now checked while they are still plain local ids - one pass over memory the packing loop walks anyway - and an overflow refuses the bake, keeps the section's game mesh, counts itself, and says so on the log with the position and the layer. The replaced records are no longer deferred on a refused replacement: the deferral belongs to the replacement, not to the attempt. Two contract tests pin both behaviours.
- **What 32 chunks really costs, measured.** The session's numbers: the 32-chunk view asks the arena for 1.09 GB, the record table's ceiling holds it at 512 MB, and until the pool fills the game meshes the rest - which at 97% device memory is the freeze. Until the distance-capped fallback lands, 16-20 chunks is the setting this device can hold.
- **Iris research updated with market evidence.** VulkanMod's own shader answer is Beryl - which ships an integrated shader pack and loads no Iris packs at all. The doc now records it: the Vulkan-native pipeline route has a working precedent, and pack compatibility remains the one unsolved hard problem (docs/iris-adaptation-research.md, section 4.5).

The distant-terrain corruption - the flat black band over the ocean - is fixed: Minecraft's own mesh now stays until the Rust bake has actually landed.

- **What the black band was, in the log's own numbers.** Minecraft's mesh for a section was dropped the moment the Rust baker accepted its payload - but accepting is queueing, and the bake queue drains at about thirty sections a second. A 32-chunk world needs tens of thousands of them, so every section sat with no game mesh and no arena geometry for minutes: a band of terrain drawn by nobody. Over an ocean that is a flat void-coloured plane where the sea should be - the corruption reported at 12 chunks in flight and at 32 chunks standing still, on every build since batching shipped.
- **The gate moved from the offer to the publish.** A section keeps Minecraft's own mesh until its bake has landed in the arena - the world is drawn by the game's own path from the first seconds, and each section hands over to the Rust terrain exactly once, when the arena can actually draw it. The publish reaches the JVM through a new per-tick drain (`publishedSections`, the mirror of the refusal drain); the first publish of a section queues one rebuild that retires the game's mesh. Refused, trimmed and parked sections all keep or regain the game's mesh - a picture drawn by the slower renderer, never a picture missing.
- **No re-bake loop.** A rebuild that retires a mesh carries no changed blocks, and a published section whose payload has nothing to say no longer calls the baker at all - so the publish drain converges instead of cycling rebuild-and-rebake forever. The per-second terrain line now separates the two states: `N of the claims published` (the arena draws them) against the claims still waiting for their bake.
- **Loading looks different on purpose.** At extreme view distances the far field stays on Minecraft's own meshes until the arena reaches it - correct and slower, and the handover is progressive rather than a band of holes. The Iris adaptation research this session produced is checked in at docs/iris-adaptation-research.md.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.31:
Same jar as the 26.1.2 release of this build; the notes describe it once.

The render-distance switch can no longer ask a phone for more memory than the draws can name.

- **What the 32-chunk report actually was, in the log's own numbers.** Switching the view to 32 chunks asked the section arena for 285,660,000 slots and was granted all of it - ten buffers, 1,216 MB - while holding 22M slots (6%, 83 MB). On a phone already carrying a 2 GB Java heap, the other 1.1 GB of granted-but-unnamed arena is what pushed the device into swap: the game at a frame a second, the launcher's own UI crawling, and the terrain beyond the near field never baked at all, because a rebuild stream that dispatches per frame cannot fill a world at one frame per second. The broken distant terrain and the near-freeze were the same event.
- **The fix: the arena stops at what the record table can name.** Every drawn section names itself through one 32,768-slot record table, and past that table's reach no amount of extra arena can be drawn - it is only memory. The arena's two sizing paths (a world joined at a distance, and a mid-session render-distance change) now hold the view's ask under a ceiling derived from that table: 512 MB, between a 21- and 22-chunk view's weight. Distances phones run (8-20 chunks) pass through untouched; 22 and up come back as the ceiling, and the growth log says so in the same line ("... the view asked for 285,660,000 asked, 134,217,728 after the record table's ceiling").
- **What 32 chunks is on a phone, honestly.** The record table caps the Rust terrain path at roughly a 24-chunk view's worth of sections; a view past that hands the excess to Minecraft's own meshes, which is correct and slower. With the arena no longer over-granted, the frame rate survives the load, the bake stream keeps up as it does at 12 chunks, and distant terrain fills in instead of staying hollow. A dense ocean world at extreme distances may still refuse sections into the vanilla path - that is the graceful answer, and it is one log line now ("N left to Minecraft because the arena is full").
- If a view still stalls on this build, the terrain lines now separate the two suspects: the arena's "holds ... for N chunk(s) of view" line (was it granted past the ceiling?) and the per-second "N left to Minecraft" count (is the record table refusing?).

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.30:
Same jar as the 26.1.2 release of this build; the notes describe it once.

The hollow-world report gets a driver interrogation of its own, and the occlusion list gets a guard against the camera moving.

- **The terrain's batched draw is now proven on the device, not assumed from the adapter.** android.29 carries each section's record in its own indices and asks nothing per draw of the driver - which is why it was taken to be beyond the reach of the first-instance probe that correctly rules the game path's batching on this one. The device then drew hollow anyway, and a probe of the old channel says nothing about the new one: a driver can break a batched call in more than one way. A second probe now runs at device creation, drawn exactly as the terrain draws - four records whose indices encode their own record, one storage table, one multi-draw - and a driver that does not draw one record per record loses the batching and keeps one draw per section, correct and slow, with both probes' answers in the log.
- **The occlusion list expires when the camera has moved out of it.** The game refills its visible-section list on a two-degree turn or an occlusion-graph update - never on movement - and a straight flight over terrain the graph has already judged leaves the list describing where the camera was. Sections the movement has since exposed are unnamed by that list, and while Minecraft's own mesh for them stays suppressed, a section neither renderer draws is a 16x16x16 hole - the other shape the hollow-world report can take. A frame whose camera has crossed out of the section the list was built in now asks the frustum about everything until the next refill; the count of such frames is in the per-second terrain line.
- **The occlusion switch moves to the Optimization section** of the renderer's own settings page, renamed in spirit: it is the switch to flip first when terrain shows holes, and its description now says so, in English and in Chinese.
- **The video settings page carries the field of view**, the one row of the game's own Display group it had not had; it lives on the General page between brightness and GUI scale, with the game's own words for 70 and 110.
- The stale experiment label and description on the Rust terrain switch are gone: it draws all three terrain layers now, and both language files say what it actually does.

If the world still draws hollow on this build, the log now says which of the three causes it was - the batched draw ("index-record probe"), the occlusion snapshot ("moved out of the section the list was built in"), or neither - and the occlusion switch is one tap away.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.20:
Stability and performance batch one: the audit round.

- The draw path's remaining crash class is closed. A draw whose vertex or index buffer slot arrives NULL, a slot the plan declares that the draw left unbound, a draw with no pipeline, and a binding table past the ABI's size are refused with a report-once line now - missing draws and a log line instead of a SIGSEGV or an abort. The same treatment reached drop_render_pass (a NULL pass drops as nothing), setMatrix (a wrong-sized array is skipped), the block registry (a malformed blockstate key or a missing atlas skips the state), the model baker (a face whose rotation is not one of the four quarter turns draws unturned), the palette bridge, entity registration, and the block bake queue.
- The translucent sort key is a 64-bit sum now: a packed position reaches 32,768 an axis, and three of those squared overflowed a 32-bit sum, which wrapped far quads into near keys and drew water out of blend order.
- Memory: the section bake no longer pins the light engine's own arrays (copied at read time), a dimension change clears the visibility table it never cleared, closed textures leave the label map, and the per-part entity state map nothing read is gone.
- Performance: the sun, the moon, the sky domes and the fog sphere are built once per scene instead of eight GPU allocations every frame; the translucent sort skips layers already in order; the per-bake winding census is sampled (every sixteenth bake); the per-draw call goes through invokeExact with no varargs array; the per-frame terrain report reads three counters instead of nine on frames that are not due; the first read of the terrain switch no longer re-meshes the world for nothing; and the pipeline precompiler can no longer write a variant into slots a reload just released.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.21:
World-black fix on Adreno 640, and the GLES option that works.

- The world was black from the first frame in it at a 12-chunk view. The section arena is bound as one storage buffer per arena, and a bind group binds a buffer entire: a 12-chunk view asked for a 192 MB pool, create_bind_group refuses any binding past max_storage_buffer_binding_size (128 MiB on the default limits), and what it leaves behind is an invalid bind group whose every use drops the whole frame - the terrain lines kept counting thousands of draws and none of them reached the GPU. The pool is split across buffers the binding can take now (128 MiB and the remainder), growth appends buffers under the same cap, and a buffer about to be bound oversized is a loud error instead of a black world.
- The renderer settings page's OpenGL ES option is attempted now instead of refused. ES 3.1 made vertex-stage storage buffers a required feature, which is what the arena reads; the attempt releases the launcher's hold on the shared window first, probes the context for vertex storage before anything is built, and falls back to Vulkan when the driver cannot. ES has no push constants, so the graph's terrain passes are not built there and the game draws its own meshes - slower than Vulkan, and the option for a device whose Vulkan driver wgpu cannot bring up.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.22:
GLES survives its first frame, and the buffers it binds are ones the driver will take.

- The GLES backend crashed at the first frame. The swapchain was configured with COPY_SRC - the usage that lets the presented image be read back for diagnostics - and a GL surface offers COLOR_TARGET only: the configure was refused, and the first acquire panicked with "Surface is not configured for presentation". The configure now asks for what the driver offers, and a driver without COPY_SRC turns the readback diagnostics off with a note instead of taking the swapchain down.
- Every ring uniform (transforms, chunk sections, lightmap, fog, cloud) and every GUI vertex buffer was refused on GLES. wgpu only lets MAP_WRITE share a usage mask with COPY_SRC unless the device advertises MAPPABLE_PRIMARY_BUFFERS - Vulkan adapters do, the GL backend never does - so on GLES the creation failed, every bind group on the buffer failed with it, and the frame drew without any of them. Nothing on this stack maps a buffer once it is created: every write travels through the staging path, so the JVM's masks are translated without the MAP bits that would sink the creation, and a mapped create is reserved for a pure staging mask. Four new tests pin the masks.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.23:
The GLES world renders.

- The GLES backend drew a black world behind a working menu: every terrain pipeline died at shader translation with "A image was used with multiple samplers". The terrain fragment shader samples one atlas through three samplers (anisotropic, nearest-magnify, minified-animated), which Vulkan's descriptor model accepts and GLES's combined sampler2D model does not - naga's GLSL writer refuses the module, the graph skips the pipelines it could not build, and the screen kept everything but the world. Each sampler now reads the atlas through its own texture binding bound to the same view, which both backends accept, so the pipelines compile and the world draws.
- A refusal the render graph's own compilation provoked was reported under the name of whichever pipeline the registry had compiled last (an android.22 log reported the terrain black screen as entity_smooth_cutout_cull and blur/5). The label the error itself carries now wins.
- An upload staged while a render pass is open recorded a copy into the command encoder that pass was borrowing - an aliasing violation that ended the process - instead of falling back to the queue-write path it now takes.
- Fewer redundant driver calls per frame: a draw whose bind groups, dynamic offsets and index buffer are already bound in the pass skips the rebind outright. Runs of draws that agree about their bindings - most of them - now cost one bind instead of one per draw.
26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.24:
The terrain draws in batches, wherever the device can carry it.

- The terrain pass drew one `draw_indexed` per section - measured at ~15,000 calls a frame on the port's phones, solid and cutout each around 7,600-8,200 at a 12-chunk view - because the `terrain_indirect` switch was off by default while the batched path was being watched. The switch is on by default now: a device that answers the three indirect feature bits draws one `multi_draw_indexed_indirect` per run of sections that share an arena, and a device that does not - GLES, a multi-draw without the count feature, DirectX 12 - keeps the per-section path with its reason in the log, exactly as before.
- The indirect buffer was sized for 10,000 draws per pass, a ceiling the 12-chunk measurement sat two-thirds of the way under and a 16-chunk view would cross - silently losing the batching while looking exactly like a device that cannot batch. The indirect args buffer now holds 24,000 records and the section-draw buffer 32,768, at about three megabytes across the three passes.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.28:
The performance release the last log pointed at: the section arena now grows to what the render distance actually asks for, and the threads this renderer owns run on the fast cores.

- **The arena grows again.** A render-distance report that arrived while the arena already held sections was supposed to grow it by appending another buffer, but the request was clamped to the size of a *single* buffer first - and on devices whose storage-binding limit makes one buffer smaller than the view (every Adreno at 12 chunks and up), the clamp left the request equal to what the arena already held, no growth was ever asked for, and sections the arena could not take were meshed by Minecraft's own path instead - the slower vertex format, drawn through the same GPU. The report is now clamped to the *pool's* ceiling (all buffers, under the memory budget), so a 12-chunk view gets the 192 MB it asks for across two buffers, and the sections that were falling back come back to the fast path.
- **Fragmentation now asks for room before it costs a section.** The growth trigger read how many slots were free; a churned arena holds its free slots as holes between held sections, so an arena at 39% held was refusing sections whose geometry had nowhere to sit - your log showed 909 of them. The trigger now also reads the longest *contiguous* free run, and appends a buffer while no run can take the largest section meshed so far. The refuse-then-re-mesh churn that shape produced is gone.
- **The render thread and the bake pool run on the performance cores.** On a big.LITTLE phone the scheduler parks whatever looks less busy on the slow cluster; the render thread now pins itself to the fast cores once, and the section-bake pool runs one thread per fast core, pinned there, leaving the efficiency cluster to the JVM's own background threads. Cluster detection is read from the device at runtime (cpufreq), and a device it cannot read keeps the old behaviour exactly.

If terrain ever goes missing after this build, that is a bug and not a culling choice - send the log. Nothing in this release changes what is drawn, only who meshes it and where it runs.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.29:
The batching release: the terrain draws in batches again on every device, including the one whose driver broke it.

- **What android.24-28 actually shipped, and what this fixes.** Every build since android.24 carried the batched terrain draw - one multi-draw indirect call per run of sections instead of one call per section - and every build since android.26 disabled it on Adreno 640, because the four-record probe this renderer runs at device creation proved that the driver accepts a non-zero `firstInstance` in an indirect record and then does not fetch the record it names. Your android.28 log says it plainly: "the first-instance probe did not read its sentinels back in order, and the terrain pass will not batch on this driver" - so the terrain kept drawing one section at a time, over a thousand calls a frame, and the 10% you measured came from the arena and core-pinning fixes alone. The batching itself never ran.
- **The record now travels in the indices.** A draw needs its section's position and its vertex range; all three previous channels for that - a storage binding indexed by `instance_index`, then an instance-step attribute offset by `first_instance` - died on the same driver. The one channel nothing can refuse is the index buffer itself: every baked index now carries the section's record slot in its high bits (`(slot << 17) | vertex`), and the vertex stage reads the record out of a per-bake table through those bits. The indirect record needs no per-draw data at all any more - `first_instance` and `base_vertex` are zero in every record, on every path, on every driver.
- **Per-frame record uploads are gone.** The records used to be rebuilt and re-uploaded for every visible section every frame (hundreds of kilobytes); they are written once per bake now, and the only per-frame upload left is the indirect argument list itself. The camera-relative offset the records used to carry is three integer subtractions in the shader.
- **The probe survives, and it guards the right thing.** The game's own repeated draws (entities, block entities) still batch through `first_instance`, so the probe now gates only that path: on a driver like this one the terrain batches and the game path draws one at a time - correct on both sides, and the terrain is the part that was slow.

Expected effect on the device the last log came from: the terrain pass goes from roughly a thousand draw calls a frame back to a handful of multi-draw calls, on top of the arena and core-pinning gains already measured. If geometry appears in the wrong place or the world draws hollow - the two signatures the old driver bug produced - send the log immediately; this build changes how every terrain vertex finds its section, and a wrong constant there is visible rather than subtle.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.36:
The world went black behind the menus on this device, and the reason was one missing flag on the section arena's usage mask.

- What the log showed: two validation errors every frame - one where the copy is encoded, one at Queue::submit - and nothing of the world drawn, while the pause menu still came up (the game's own encoder is a different one). The compacted terrain draw - the path that puts the whole frame into one draw_indexed on the drivers that refuse the batched call - blits the frame's index ranges out of the section arena into a per-frame buffer before the terrain pass opens. The arena's mask said 'no COPY_SRC': a flag dropped back when nothing copied an arena whole, which stopped being true the day the compacted draw landed. The first failed copy invalidates the frame's encoder, and a refused submission draws nothing at all.
- The mask carries COPY_SRC again, and the contract is a test now: the arena must stay a superset of what every reader asks of it - storage for the shader's fetch, vertices and indices for the draws, a copy source for the frame's blits.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.37:
Two render-distance bugs, both found in the log of the session that hit them.

- Toggling the render distance (32 to 12 and back) appended a 128 MiB arena buffer every time, and the memory walked the phone into swap: 512 -> 640 -> 768 -> 896 MB across three toggles of a view the first report had already covered, and the whole system crawled. The report used to ask for growth with the pool doubled (`pool * 2`), which is past the pool by construction - so every report was a growth ask, and every ask was answered with another arena. The ask now carries the view's own size, and a pool that already covers it asks for nothing at all; a refusal (a section that genuinely did not fit) still grows the way it did.
- Shrinking the view did not take effect until the player walked across a section boundary. The trim that drops sections beyond the view only ran when the camera changed section, and the video settings do not move the camera - so the sections between the old and the new distance stayed in the arena and kept drawing (the same camera drew 749 sections a frame where its first 12-chunk view had drawn 475). A width change now makes the trim due on its own, the dropped sections are handed back the way refusals are, and Minecraft's own meshes take over beyond the new edge.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.42:
The terrain draws straight out of the arena, and the phone presents every frame it makes.

- **The gathering now prefers drawing in place.** The compacted draw - the shape every probe-refusing device runs - merges the frame's sections into contiguous runs, and then *copies* their index ranges into a per-frame buffer to draw them as one call. But a run that is already contiguous where it lives needs no copy at all: it is one plain `draw_indexed` over its own slice of the arena. That shape is the first choice now, the compacted draw (and its 16 MB buffers, which the logs watched grow 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8 -> 16 MB per slot) only takes over when a pass fragments past 256 runs, and a once-a-second line names any pass that crosses. While moving - exactly when the copies used to land every frame - the blit bytes are gone, on every GPU, both vendors included.
- **vsync defaults off now** (the same defaults migration that carried the batching switch onto older configs, revision 2). Fifo, what vsync asks for, is a double-buffered queue: a frame that misses the display's refresh waits for the *next* one, so a GPU rendering at 45 fps presents at 30 - which reads as half the framerate the hardware should manage. The devices whose configs carry the old default get it flipped once; turning vsync back on holds from there. If a device still feels below its hardware after this update, check this switch first.
- The batching probes print their evidence. Both probes - first-instance and index-record - have been failing on Adreno 640 *and* Mali-G610, which is two vendors answering one question the same wrong way and no log line saying what any of them saw. A failed probe now prints the four words it read back: a collapsed call reads 100 four times, a dead fetch zeros, an unrun one the clear colour - and the next log names which of these it is, or something new.

26.1.1.2612.0.8-android.52:
The renderer answers the FSR question the device has been asking: the frame is now rendered at a fraction of the window's resolution and stretched back over it, sharpened - the largest frame-time lever a phone has left.

- **Render scale (new setting, default 0.75 on Android, 1.0 elsewhere).** Everything the game draws - terrain, entities, water, sky, GUI - goes into one render target, and a tiler's fragment cost is per pixel: rendering at 0.75 hands back roughly forty percent of that work, which is the difference the far-field sampling change only began. 1.0 is the un-scaled picture, sampled one-to-one, exactly what previous builds made. Set it in the mod's own settings screen; it applies the moment Apply is pressed.
- **Upscale sharpening (new setting, default 0.5).** The present blit stretches the scaled frame back over the window with an unsharp mask over each sample's neighbourhood, so the picture keeps the crispness the window's own resolution would have had. It only does something while the render scale is below 1.0.
- The game's GUI stays laid out by the window as it always was and is drawn proportionally, a little softer by the scale; touch and aim are unaffected - the window never changes size. Lower the scale to 0.6-0.7 for more frames on an older GPU, or back to 1.0 for the exact old picture.

Same jar as the 26.1.2 release of this build; the notes describe it once.

- **What you saw: a world of stretched, shredded triangles.** android.40 rounded every arena allocation to a multiple of four words so the terrain shaders could load vertices as whole vectors - the change that fixed the per-vertex load storm. But six indices a quad only lands on a four-word boundary for every second section, so the odd sections carried two spare words at the end of their index range, holding whatever the previous section had left there. One section drawing alone never completed a triangle out of them. The compacted draw - the path this renderer's phones actually draw with - packs sections back to back into one index buffer, and those two words sat *between* two sections' real indices: from the first slack word on, every triangle of the run was three wrong vertices, and the two spare words themselves were stale index values pointing into recycled sections. A world of long black spikes is what that reads as.
- **The fix: draws measure indices exactly as baked.** The allocation stays rounded - that is the vec4 contract, and the shaders lean on it - but the exact baked count now travels beside it, and every consumer measures draws with it: the compacted draw's copies and destinations, the one-draw-per-section fallback, the batched indirect records. A section's indices now end in the buffer exactly where the next section's begin, and every triangle the GPU reads is a quad the bake wrote.
- **Pinned by tests so it cannot come back quietly**: the arena records both counts and the gap between them, and the copy planner asserts every section's destination lands on a triangle boundary.

The arena's vertex data is now loaded one whole vector per vertex, and the bake packs the four corner counts into one word per quad that all four vertices share; the section record moved to two whole vectors for the same reason. This is the one stage that runs per vertex, and load/store pressure there is what tile-based mobile GPUs (Mali in particular) are shortest of - this is the change aimed at the 'performance does not match the hardware' gap, not a tweak.

Standing still or turning in place in a settled world, the copies drop to zero; a bake, a trim, or a pool change moves the counter and the copies come back for that frame. The stretched-terrain corruption - long thin triangles shooting into the sky while a world loads - is closed on the renderer's own paths, and both fixes count and log themselves so a field log can name any remaining culprit.

- **Where the streaks came from.** A baked index is `(record_slot << 17) | local_vertex`, and the shader reads the section's record out of the high bits. Two ways to draw wrong geometry: a bake whose local vertex id ran past the 17 bits the format holds (the guard for this was a `debug_assert`, which a release build compiles away - the spill silently shifted the record slot and fetched another section's vertices at this one's transform), and a rebuild the pool refused whose replaced record slots were freed anyway - the kept section then read whoever took the slot next. Both are exactly the picture the 32-chunk screenshot showed: triangles stretched across the world, chunks in the wrong place, black fragments.
- **The fixes.** Every bake's indices are now checked while they are still plain local ids - one pass over memory the packing loop walks anyway - and an overflow refuses the bake, keeps the section's game mesh, counts itself, and says so on the log with the position and the layer. The replaced records are no longer deferred on a refused replacement: the deferral belongs to the replacement, not to the attempt. Two contract tests pin both behaviours.
- **What 32 chunks really costs, measured.** The session's numbers: the 32-chunk view asks the arena for 1.09 GB, the record table's ceiling holds it at 512 MB, and until the pool fills the game meshes the rest - which at 97% device memory is the freeze. Until the distance-capped fallback lands, 16-20 chunks is the setting this device can hold.

The doc now records it: the Vulkan-native pipeline route has a working precedent, and pack compatibility remains the one unsolved hard problem (docs/iris-adaptation-research.md, section 4.5).

- **What the black band was, in the log's own numbers.** Minecraft's mesh for a section was dropped the moment the Rust baker accepted its payload - but accepting is queueing, and the bake queue drains at about thirty sections a second. A 32-chunk world needs tens of thousands of them, so every section sat with no game mesh and no arena geometry for minutes: a band of terrain drawn by nobody. Over an ocean that is a flat void-coloured plane where the sea should be - the corruption reported at 12 chunks in flight and at 32 chunks standing still, on every build since batching shipped.
- **The gate moved from the offer to the publish.** A section keeps Minecraft's own mesh until its bake has landed in the arena - the world is drawn by the game's own path from the first seconds, and each section hands over to the Rust terrain exactly once, when the arena can actually draw it. The publish reaches the JVM through a new per-tick drain (`publishedSections`, the mirror of the refusal drain); the first publish of a section queues one rebuild that retires the game's mesh. Refused, trimmed and parked sections all keep or regain the game's mesh - a picture drawn by the slower renderer, never a picture missing.
- **No re-bake loop.** A rebuild that retires a mesh carries no changed blocks, and a published section whose payload has nothing to say no longer calls the baker at all - so the publish drain converges instead of cycling rebuild-and-rebake forever. The per-second terrain line now separates the two states: `N of the claims published` (the arena draws them) against the claims still waiting for their bake.
- **Loading looks different on purpose.** At extreme view distances the far field stays on Minecraft's own meshes until the arena reaches it - correct and slower, and the handover is progressive rather than a band of holes. The Iris adaptation research this session produced is checked in at docs/iris-adaptation-research.md.

On a phone already carrying a 2 GB Java heap, the other 1.1 GB of granted-but-unnamed arena is what pushed the device into swap: the game at a frame a second, the launcher's own UI crawling, and the terrain beyond the near field never baked at all, because a rebuild stream that dispatches per frame cannot fill a world at one frame per second. The broken distant terrain and the near-freeze were the same event.
- **The fix: the arena stops at what the record table can name.** Every drawn section names itself through one 32,768-slot record table, and past that table's reach no amount of extra arena can be drawn - it is only memory. The arena's two sizing paths (a world joined at a distance, and a mid-session render-distance change) now hold the view's ask under a ceiling derived from that table: 512 MB, between a 21- and 22-chunk view's weight. Distances phones run (8-20 chunks) pass through untouched; 22 and up come back as the ceiling, and the growth log says so in the same line ("... the view asked for 285,660,000 asked, 134,217,728 after the record table's ceiling").
- **What 32 chunks is on a phone, honestly.** The record table caps the Rust terrain path at roughly a 24-chunk view's worth of sections; a view past that hands the excess to Minecraft's own meshes, which is correct and slower. With the arena no longer over-granted, the frame rate survives the load, the bake stream keeps up as it does at 12 chunks, and distant terrain fills in instead of staying hollow. A dense ocean world at extreme distances may still refuse sections into the vanilla path - that is the graceful answer, and it is one log line now ("N left to Minecraft because the arena is full").
- If a view still stalls on this build, the terrain lines now separate the two suspects: the arena's "holds ... for N chunk(s) of view" line (was it granted past the ceiling?) and the per-second "N left to Minecraft" count (is the record table refusing?).

Nothing on this stack maps a buffer once it is created: every write travels through the staging path, so the JVM's masks are translated without the MAP bits that would sink the creation, and a mapped create is reserved for a pure staging mask.
